[[File:Kepler-solar-system-2.png|thumb|286x286px|The [[Platonic solid]]s, seen here in an illustration from [[Johannes Kepler]]'s ''[[Mysterium Cosmographicum]]'' (1596), are an early example of exceptional objects. The symmetries of three-dimensional space can be classified into two infinite families—the [[Cyclic group|cyclic]] and [[Dihedral group|dihedral]] symmetries of ''n''-sided polygons—and five exceptional types of symmetry, namely the symmetry groups of the Platonic solids.]]

In [[mathematics]], an '''exceptional object''' is one of finitely many exceptions to some classification of objects. Many branches of mathematics study objects of a given type and prove a [[classification theorem]]. A common theme is that the classification results in a number of series of objects and a finite number of exceptions — often with desirable properties — that do not fit into any series; these are known as exceptional objects. In many cases, these exceptional objects play a further and important role in the subject. Furthermore, the exceptional objects in one branch of mathematics often relate to the exceptional objects in others.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stillwell|first=John|date=1998|title=Exceptional Objects|jstor=2589218|journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]|volume=105|issue=9|pages=850–858|doi=10.2307/2589218}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite arXiv|eprint=1505.06742|first1=Yang-Hui|last1=He|first2=John|last2=McKay|author-link2=John McKay (mathematician)|title=Sporadic and Exceptional|date=25 May 2015|class=math.AG}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plus.maths.org/content/os/issue33/features/baez/index|title=Ubiquitous octonions|last=Joyce|first=Helen|date=1 January 2005|website=Plus Magazine|language=en|access-date=2017-08-06}}</ref>

A related phenomenon is [[exceptional isomorphism]], when two series are in general different, but agree for some small values. For example, [[spin group]]s in low dimensions are [[isomorphism|isomorphic]] to other [[classical Lie group]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/exceptional+isomorphism|title=exceptional isomorphism in nLab|website=ncatlab.org|access-date=2019-11-29}}</ref>

== Regular polytopes ==
{{Main|Regular polytope}}
The prototypical examples of exceptional objects arise in the classification of [[regular polytope]]s: in two dimensions, there is a series of [[regular polygon|regular ''n''-gons]] for ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;3. In every dimension above 2, one can find analogues of the cube, tetrahedron and octahedron. In three dimensions, one finds two more regular polyhedra — the [[dodecahedron]] (12-hedron) and the [[icosahedron]] (20-hedron) — making five [[Platonic solids]]. In four dimensions, a total of six [[Convex regular 4-polytope|regular polytopes]] exist, including the [[120-cell]], the [[600-cell]] and the [[24-cell]]. There are no other regular polytopes, as the only regular polytopes in higher dimensions are of the [[hypercube]], [[simplex]], [[orthoplex]] series. In all dimensions combined, there are therefore three series and five exceptional polytopes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/platonic.html|title=Platonic Solids in All Dimensions|last=Baez|first=John C.|date=12 November 2006|website=math.ucr.edu|access-date=2017-08-07}}</ref>

Moreover, the pattern is similar if non-convex polytopes are included: in two dimensions, there is a [[regular star polygon]] for every [[rational number]] <math>\textstyle p/q>2</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/StarPolygon.html|title=Star Polygon|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|language=en|access-date=2019-11-29}}</ref>  In three dimensions, there are four [[Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron|Kepler–Poinsot polyhedra]], and in four dimensions, ten [[Schläfli–Hess polychoron|Schläfli–Hess polychora]]; in higher dimensions, there are no non-convex regular figures.

These can be generalized to [[tessellation]]s of other spaces, especially [[Uniform tiling|uniform tessellations]], notably tilings of Euclidean space ([[honeycomb (geometry)|honeycombs]]), which have exceptional objects, and tilings of hyperbolic space. There are various exceptional objects in dimension below 6, but in dimension 6 and above, the only regular polyhedra/tilings/hyperbolic tilings are the simplex, hypercube, cross-polytope, and hypercube lattice.

=== Schwarz triangles ===
{{further|Schwarz triangle}}
{| class="wikitable" align=right
|[[File:Sphere symmetry group td.svg|120px]]<BR>(3 3 2)
|[[File:Sphere symmetry group oh.svg|120px]]<BR>(4 3 2)

|-
|[[File:Tile 3,6.svg|120px]]<BR>(3 3 3)
|[[File:Tile V488 bicolor.svg|120px]]<BR>(4 4 2)

Related to tilings and the regular polyhedra, there are exceptional [[Schwarz triangle]]s (triangles that tile the sphere, or more generally Euclidean plane or hyperbolic plane via their [[triangle group]] of reflections in their edges), particularly the [[Möbius triangle]]s. In the sphere, there are 3 Möbius triangles (and 1 1-parameter family), corresponding to the 3 exceptional Platonic solid groups, while in the Euclidean plane, there are 3 Möbius triangles, corresponding to the 3 special triangles: 60-60-60 ([[equilateral triangle|equilateral]]), [[45-45-90]] (isosceles right), and [[30-60-90]]. There are additional exceptional Schwarz triangles in the sphere and Euclidean plane. By contrast, in the hyperbolic plane, there is a 3-parameter family of Möbius triangles, and none exceptional.

== Finite simple groups ==
{{Main|Sporadic group}}
[[File:SporadicGroups.svg|thumb|The relations between the sporadic groups, most being related to the monster.]]

The finite simple groups have been [[Classification of finite simple groups|classified]] into a number of series as well as 26 [[sporadic groups]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plus.maths.org/content/enormous-theorem-classification-finite-simple-groups|title=An enormous theorem: the classification of finite simple groups|date=2006-12-07|website=plus.maths.org|language=en|access-date=2019-11-29}}</ref> Of these, 20 are subgroups or subquotients of the [[monster group]], referred to as the "Happy Family", while 6 are not, and are referred to as "[[Pariah group|pariahs]]".

Several of the sporadic groups are related to the [[Leech lattice]], most notably the Conway group Co<sub>1</sub>, which is the automorphism group of the Leech lattice, quotiented out by its center.

== Division algebras ==

There are only three finite-dimensional associative [[division algebra]]s over the reals — the [[real numbers]], the [[complex numbers]] and the [[quaternions]]. The only non-associative division algebra is the algebra of [[octonions]]. The octonions are connected to a wide variety of exceptional objects. For example, the exceptional formally real [[Jordan algebra]] is the [[Albert algebra]] of 3×3 self-adjoint matrices over the octonions.

== Simple Lie groups ==

The [[simple Lie group]]s form a number of series ([[classical Lie group]]s) labelled A, B, C and D. In addition, there are the exceptional groups [[G2 (mathematics)|G<sub>2</sub>]] (the automorphism group of the octonions), [[F4 (mathematics)|F<sub>4</sub>]], [[E6 (mathematics)|E<sub>6</sub>]], [[E7 (mathematics)|E<sub>7</sub>]], [[E8 (mathematics)|E<sub>8</sub>]]. These last four groups can be viewed as the symmetry groups of projective planes over '''O''', '''C'''⊗'''O''', '''H'''⊗'''O''' and '''O'''⊗'''O''', respectively, where '''O''' is the octonions and the tensor products are over the reals.

The classification of Lie groups corresponds to the classification of [[root systems]], and thus the exceptional Lie groups correspond to exceptional root systems and exceptional [[Dynkin diagram]]s.

== Supersymmetric algebras ==
There are a few exceptional objects with [[supersymmetry]]. The classification of [[superalgebra]]s by [[Victor Kac|Kac]] and Tierry-Mieg indicates that the [[Lie superalgebra]]s '''G(3)''' in 31 dimensions and '''F(4)''' in 40 dimensions, and the Jordan superalgebras '''K<sub>3</sub>''' and '''K<sub>10</sub>''', are examples of exceptional objects.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kac|first=V. G.|date=1977-01-01|title=Classification of simple z-graded lie superalgebras and simple jordan superalgebras|journal=Communications in Algebra|volume=5|issue=13|pages=1375–1400|doi=10.1080/00927877708822224|issn=0092-7872}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Group Theoretical Methods in Physics|volume = 201|last=Thierry-Mieg|first=Jean|date=1984|publisher=Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg|pages=94–98|language=en|doi=10.1007/bfb0016126|chapter = Irreducible representations of the basic classical Lie superalgebras SU(m/n) ; SU(n/n)/U(1) ; OSp(m/2n) ; D(2/1 ; α ) ; G(3) ; F(4)|series = Lecture Notes in Physics|isbn = 978-3-540-13335-3}}</ref>

== Unimodular lattices ==

Up to isometry, there is only one even [[unimodular lattice]] in 15 dimensions or less &mdash; the [[E8 lattice|E<sub>8</sub> lattice]]. Up to dimension [[24 (number)|24]], there is only one even unimodular lattice without [[root system|roots]], the [[Leech lattice]]. Three of the sporadic simple groups were discovered by Conway while investigating the automorphism group of the Leech lattice. For example, [[Conway group|Co<sub>1</sub>]] is the automorphism group itself modulo ±1. The groups [[Conway group|Co<sub>2</sub>]] and [[Conway group|Co<sub>3</sub>]], as well as a number of other sporadic groups, arise as stabilisers of various subsets of the Leech lattice.

== Codes ==

Some [[Error-correcting code|codes]] also stand out as exceptional objects, in particular the perfect binary Golay code, which is closely related to the Leech lattice. The [[Mathieu group]] <math>M_{24}</math>, one of the sporadic simple groups, is the group of automorphisms of the [[binary Golay code|extended binary Golay code]], and four more of the sporadic simple groups arise as various types of stabilizer subgroup of <math>M_{24}</math>.

== Block designs ==

An exceptional [[block design]] is the [[Steiner system]] S(5,8,24) whose automorphism group is the sporadic simple [[Mathieu group]] <math>M_{24}</math>.

The codewords of the [[binary Golay code|extended binary Golay code]] have a length of 24 bits and have weights 0, 8, 12, 16, or 24. This code can correct up to three errors. So every 24-bit word with weight 5 can be corrected to a codeword with weight 8. The bits of a 24-bit word can be thought of as specifying the possible subsets of a 24 element set. So the extended binary Golay code gives a unique 8 element subset for each 5 element subset. In fact, it defines S(5,8,24).

== Outer automorphisms ==
Certain families of groups often have a certain [[outer automorphism group]], but in particular cases, they have other exceptional outer automorphisms.

Among families of finite simple groups, the only example is in the [[automorphisms of the symmetric and alternating groups]]: for <math>n \geq 3, n \neq 6</math> the [[alternating group]] <math>A_n</math> has one outer automorphism (corresponding to conjugation by an odd element of <math>S_n</math>) and the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math> has no outer automorphisms. However, for <math>n=6,</math> there is an [[Automorphisms of the symmetric and alternating groups#exceptional outer automorphism|exceptional outer automorphism]] of <math>S_6</math> (of order 2), and correspondingly, the outer automorphism group of <math>A_6</math> is not <math>C_2</math> (the group of order 2), but rather <math>C_2 \times C_2</math>, the [[Klein four-group]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://golem.ph.utexas.edu/category/2015/08/a_wrinkle_in_the_mathematical.html|title=A Wrinkle in the Mathematical Universe|last=Baez|first=John C.|date=17 August 2015|website=[[nLab|The n-Category Café]]|access-date=2017-08-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://brauer.maths.qmul.ac.uk/Atlas/v3/alt/A6/|title=ATLAS: Alternating group A6, Linear group L2(9), Symplectic group S4(2)', Mathieu group M10'|website=[[Atlas of Finite Groups|Atlas of Finite Group Representations]]|language=en|access-date=2017-08-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lYMAg_Sj7hUC|title=The Finite Simple Groups|last=Wilson|first=Robert|date=2009-12-14|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781848009875|pages=19|language=en}}</ref>

If one instead considers <math>A_6</math> as the (isomorphic) [[projective special linear group]] <math>\operatorname{PSL}(2,9) </math>, then the outer automorphism is not exceptional; thus the exceptional-ness can be seen as due to the [[exceptional isomorphism]] <math>A_6 \cong \operatorname{PSL}(2,9).</math> This exceptional outer automorphism is realized inside of the Mathieu group <math>M_{12}</math> and similarly, <math>M_{12}</math> acts on a set of 12 elements in 2 different ways.

{{Gallery
|File:Tutte-Coxeter graph 2COL.svg|alt1=Tutte–Coxeter graph|The [[Tutte–Coxeter graph]]: the symmetries of this graph are the automorphisms of ''S''<sub>6</sub>. The exceptional automorphism corresponds to swapping the colors of the blue and red vertices.<ref name=":0"/>
|File:Dynkin diagram D4.png|alt2=The D4 Dynkin diagram|The symmetries of the Dynkin diagram D<sub>4</sub> correspond to the [[outer automorphism]]s of Spin(8) in triality.
|align=center
}}

Among [[Lie groups]], the [[spin group]] <math>\operatorname{Spin}(8)</math> has an exceptionally large outer automorphism group (namely <math>S_3</math>), which corresponds to the exceptional symmetries of the [[Dynkin diagram]] <math>D_4</math>. This phenomenon is referred to as ''[[triality]].''

The exceptional symmetry of the <math>D_4</math> diagram also gives rise to the [[Steinberg group (Lie theory)|Steinberg groups]].

== Algebraic topology ==
{{Main|Kervaire invariant}}
The [[Kervaire invariant]] is an invariant of a (4''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2)-dimensional manifold that measures whether the manifold could be [[Surgery theory|surgically]] converted into a sphere. This invariant evaluates to 0 if the manifold can be converted to a sphere, and 1 otherwise. More specifically, the Kervaire invariant applies to a [[framed manifold]], that is, to a manifold equipped with an [[embedding]] into [[Euclidean space]] and a trivialization of the [[normal bundle]]. The Kervaire invariant problem is the problem of determining in which dimensions the Kervaire invariant can be nonzero. For differentiable manifolds, this can happen in dimensions 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, and possibly 126, and in no other dimensions. The final case of dimension 126 remains open.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/mathematics-and-physical-science/mathematicians-solve-45-year-old-kervaire-invariant-puzzle/|title=Mathematicians Solve 45-Year-Old Kervaire Invariant Puzzle|last=Klarreich|first=Erica|date=20 July 2009|website=[[Simons Foundation]]|language=en-US|access-date=2017-08-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite arXiv|eprint=1104.4523|first=Haynes|last=Miller|author-link=Haynes Miller|title=Kervaire Invariant One [after M. A. Hill, M. J. Hopkins, and D. C. Ravenel]|date=5 June 2012|class=math.AT}}</ref> These five or six framed [[cobordism class]]es of manifolds having Kervaire invariant 1 are exceptional objects related to [[exotic sphere]]s. The first three cases are related to the complex numbers, quaternions and octonions respectively: a manifold of Kervaire invariant 1 can be constructed as the product of two spheres, with its exotic framing determined by the normed division algebra.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ranicki|first=Andrew|date=2011|title=Commentary on "On the parallelizability of the spheres" by R. Bott and J. Milnor and "On the nonexistence of elements of Hopf invariant one" by J. F. Adams|url=https://www.ams.org/bull/2011-48-04/S0273-0979-2011-01345-3/|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|volume=48|issue=4|pages=509–511|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-2011-01345-3|issn=0273-0979|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Due to similarities of dimensions, it is conjectured that the remaining cases (dimensions 30, 62 and 126) are related to the [[Rosenfeld projective plane]]s, which are defined over algebras constructed from the octonions. Specifically, it has been conjectured that there is a construction that takes these projective planes and produces a manifold with nonzero Kervaire invariant in two dimensions lower, but this remains unconfirmed.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://math.northwestern.edu/~ebelmont/talbot-notes-2016.pdf |title=Talbot 2016: Equivariant homotopy theory and the Kervaire invariant one problem |last=Belmont |first=Eva |date=2016-05-16 |access-date=2020-04-18 |website=math.northwestern.edu}}</ref>

== Symmetric quantum measurements ==

In [[quantum information science|quantum information theory]], there exist structures known as [[SIC-POVM]]s or SICs, which correspond to maximal sets of complex [[equiangular lines]]. Some of the known SICs&mdash;those in vector spaces of 2 and 3 dimensions, as well as certain solutions in 8 dimensions&mdash;are considered exceptional objects and called "sporadic SICs". They differ from the other known SICs in ways that involve their symmetry groups, the [[Galois theory]] of the numerical values of their vector components, and so forth.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Appleby|first1=Marcus|last2=Flammia|first2=Steven|last3=McConnell|first3=Gary|last4=Yard|first4=Jon|date=2017-08-01|title=SICs and Algebraic Number Theory|journal=Foundations of Physics|language=en|volume=47|issue=8|pages=1042–1059|arxiv=1701.05200|doi=10.1007/s10701-017-0090-7|issn=0015-9018|bibcode=2017FoPh...47.1042A|s2cid=119334103}}</ref> The sporadic SICs in dimension 8 are related to the integral octonions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Stacey|first=Blake C.|date=2017-08-01|title=Sporadic SICs and the Normed Division Algebras|journal=Foundations of Physics|language=en|volume=47|issue=8|pages=1060–1064|arxiv=1605.01426|doi=10.1007/s10701-017-0087-2|issn=0015-9018|bibcode=2017FoPh...47.1060S|s2cid=118438232}}</ref>

== Connections ==
Numerous connections have been observed between some, though not all, of these exceptional objects. Most common are objects related to [[8 (number)|8]] and [[24 (number)|24]] dimensions, noting that 24&nbsp;=&nbsp;8&nbsp;·&nbsp;3.  By contrast, the [[pariah group]]s stand apart, as the name suggests.

=== 8 and 24 dimensions ===
Exceptional objects related to the number 8 include the following.
* The octonions are 8-dimensional.
* The [[E8 lattice|E<sub>8</sub> lattice]] can be realized as the integral octonions (up to a scale factor).
* The exceptional Lie groups can be seen as symmetries of the octonions and structures derived from the octonions;<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/week106.html|title=This Week's Finds in Mathematical Physics: Week106|last=Baez|first=John C.|date=23 July 1997|website=math.ucr.edu|access-date=2017-08-07}}</ref> further, the E<sub>8</sub> algebra is related to the E<sub>8</sub> lattice, as the notation implies (the lattice is generated by the root system of the algebra).
* Triality occurs for Spin(8), which also connects to 8&nbsp;·&nbsp;3 &nbsp;=&nbsp;24.
Likewise, exceptional objects related to the number 24 include the following.
* The Leech lattice is 24-dimensional.
* Most sporadic simple groups can be related to the Leech lattice, or more broadly the Monster.
* The exceptional [[Jordan algebra]] has a representation in terms of 24&times;24 real matrices together with the Jordan product rule.

These objects are connected to various other phenomena in math which may be considered surprising but not themselves "exceptional". For example, in [[algebraic topology]], 8-fold real [[Bott periodicity]] can be seen as coming from the octonions. In the theory of [[modular forms]], the 24-dimensional nature of the Leech lattice underlies the presence of 24 in the formulas for the [[Dedekind eta function]] and the [[modular discriminant]], which connection is deepened by [[Monstrous moonshine]], a development that related modular functions to the Monster group.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Borcherds|first=Richard E.|author-link=Richard Borcherds|date=1998|title=What is Moonshine?|url=http://www.emis.de/journals/DMJDMV/xvol-icm/Fields/Borcherds.MAN.html|journal=Documenta Mathematica|volume=ICM 1|pages=607&ndash;615|arxiv=math/9809110|bibcode=1998math......9110B}}</ref>

=== Physics ===
In [[string theory]] and superstring theory we often find that particular dimensions are singled out as a result of exceptional algebraic phenomena. For example, [[bosonic string theory]] requires a spacetime of dimension 26 which is directly related to the presence of 24 in the [[Dedekind eta function]]. Similarly, the possible dimensions of [[supergravity]] are related to the dimensions of the [[division algebra]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baez|first1=John C.|last2=Huerta|first2=John|date=October 2011|title=Division algebras and supersymmetry II|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.atmp/1349879112|journal=Advances in Theoretical and Mathematical Physics|language=EN|volume=15|issue=5|pages=1373–1410|arxiv=1003.3436|issn=1095-0761|doi=10.4310/atmp.2011.v15.n5.a4|s2cid=10270325}}</ref>

=== Monstrous moonshine ===

Many of the exceptional objects in mathematics and physics have been found to be connected to each other. Developments such as the [[Monstrous moonshine]] conjectures show how, for example, the [[Monster group]] is connected to [[string theory]]. The theory of [[modular forms]] shows how the algebra E<sub>8</sub> is connected to the Monster group. (In fact, well before the proof of the Monstrous moonshine conjecture, the [[J-invariant|elliptic ''j''-function]] was discovered to encode the representations of E<sub>8</sub>.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kac|first=V.G|title=An elucidation of "Infinite-Dimensional Algebras … and the very strange formula." E(1)8 and the cube root of the modular invariant j|journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]|volume=35|issue=3|pages=264–273|doi=10.1016/0001-8708(80)90052-3|year=1980|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kac|first=V.G|title=Infinite-dimensional algebras, Dedekind's η-function, classical möbius function and the very strange formula|journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]|volume=30|issue=2|pages=85–136|doi=10.1016/0001-8708(78)90033-6|year=1978|doi-access=}}</ref>) Other interesting connections include how the [[Leech lattice]] is connected via the [[Binary Golay code|Golay code]] to the adjacency matrix of the [[dodecahedron]] (another exceptional object). Below is a [[mind map]] showing how some of the exceptional objects in mathematics and [[mathematical physics]] are related.

[[File:Exceptionalmindmap2.png|600px]]

The connections can partly be explained by thinking of the algebras as a tower of lattice [[vertex operator algebra]]s. It just so happens that the vertex algebras at the bottom are so simple that they are isomorphic to familiar non-vertex algebras. Thus the connections can be seen simply as the consequence of some lattices being sub-lattices of others.

=== Supersymmetries ===
The [[Jordan superalgebra]]s are a parallel set of exceptional objects with [[supersymmetry]]. These are the [[Lie superalgebra]]s which are related to Lorentzian lattices. This subject is less explored, and the connections between the objects are less well established. There are new conjectures parallel to the [[Monstrous moonshine]] conjectures for these super-objects, involving different sporadic groups.{{Citation needed|date=August 2017}}

[[File:supermindmap.png|550px]]

== Unexceptional objects ==

=== Pathologies ===
{{See also|Pathological (mathematics)}}
"Exceptional" object is reserved for objects that are unusual, meaning rare, the exception, not for ''unexpected'' or ''non-standard'' objects. These unexpected-but-typical (or common) phenomena are generally referred to as [[Pathological (mathematics)|pathological]], such as [[nowhere differentiable function]]s, or "exotic", as in [[exotic sphere]]s — there are exotic spheres in arbitrarily high dimension (not only a [[finite set]] of exceptions), and in many dimensions most (differential structures on) spheres are exotic.

=== Extremal objects ===
Exceptional objects must be distinguished from ''extremal'' objects: those that fall in a family and are the most extreme example by some measure are of interest, but not unusual in the way exceptional objects are. For example, the [[golden ratio]] ''φ'' has the simplest [[simple continued fraction|continued fraction approximation]], and accordingly is most difficult to [[Diophantine approximation|approximate by rationals]]; however, it is but one of infinitely many such quadratic numbers (continued fractions).

Similarly, the (2,3,7) [[Schwarz triangle]] is the smallest hyperbolic Schwarz triangle, and the associated [[(2,3,7) triangle group]] is of particular interest, being the universal [[Hurwitz group]], and thus being associated with the [[Hurwitz curve]]s, the maximally symmetric algebraic curves. However, it falls in a family of such triangles ((2,4,7), (2,3,8), (3,3,7), etc.), and while the smallest, is not exceptional or unlike the others.
